title: CQRS and read models
subtitle: Split the model you write with from the models you read from, keep each read model rebuildable, and design the screen for the moments when it lags.

c.v: On 1 April 2026, GitHub code search failed every query from 14:40 to 17:00 UTC. That is the report's timeline. Its header lists the incident from 15:02.

It started with a routine upgrade to the messaging system behind search. An automated change was applied too aggressively. Internal services lost coordination, search indexing stopped, and results began to go stale.
During recovery, an unintended deployment cleared internal routing state. That turned stale search into no search at all.
At 17:00 search came back, but in a degraded state. Results did not show any repository change made after about 07:00 UTC. Search only showed current data again at 23:45.
The fix is the interesting part. The team reset the search index to a point before the problem, and indexed again from there.
No repository data was lost. The report explains why: the search index is a
derived from the Git repositories, and those were not affected.
. It could be wrong for hours, and then be rebuilt from the source of truth.
Most code uses one model for everything. The same
class and table handle "ship this order" and "show my last 20 orders".

Fowler first heard the idea from Greg Young.

The write model checks the rules and saves the change.

The two models may share one database, or use separate ones.
With separate stores, you can pick a different technology for each, such as a relational write store and a document read store.

The write model is the truth. Every read model is a disposable copy, shaped for one kind of read. Make each copy easy to rebuild, and design the screen for the time when it is behind.

Each one lags by a different amount, and each needs its own rebuild plan.

A projection reads events in order and remembers how far it got. In KurrentDB you subscribe from a stored position. To resume after a restart, you must save the position of the last event you handled. That saved position is a checkpoint.
Marten's projection daemon stores its progress too. When a
stops, it flushes its progress row, so the next start "picks up exactly where this one left off".
A crash after you apply an event, but before you save the checkpoint, replays that event. So the handler must be idempotent.
Order matters within one aggregate. "Shipped" before "Paid" would leave the wrong status. Route all events of one order to one handler at a time. With Kafka, you key messages by order ID, as in
. Order across different orders rarely matters.
Store the last applied version on each read-model row. Then a duplicate or an old event is easy to spot. Step through it. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.

Building next to the old table and swapping is your job.
Keep readers on the old view while the new one builds. Microsoft's advice is to build and validate the new view, then swap to it.
GitHub's recovery was the same idea at scale: go back to a known good point and index forward.
Time a full rebuild before you need one. If it takes two days, you need snapshots or a faster path. Microsoft notes that building views from many events can cost a lot of time and compute.
After a user's command, the read model is behind for a moment. Microsoft calls this out: the read side may not show the newest changes at once.

In a UI, wait a second or two, then show "updating…".
Also watch lag in production. Microsoft warns that a lost or late refresh signal makes a view serve stale results with no error. Alert when its age passes your limit.
Most services. Fowler says many systems fit CRUD.

Fowler's warning is blunt: "for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity". Use it only on specific parts of a system.
Microsoft adds that it may not suit simple domains, or apps where CRUD screens are enough.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "Which screen is slow or awkward, and why?"
Often an index or a reporting
For every read model, write down its owner, its source, its usual lag and how to rebuild it. Time the rebuild.
Put a version on every read-model row and on every command reply. It costs one column and makes duplicates and stale reads easy to spot.
Never let a command handler write the read model in a second call. That is a
Alert on projection lag in seconds, and on handlers stuck on one event.
Design each screen for lag. Decide what the user sees during the first second after they act.
When a read model is wrong, rebuild it next to the old one and swap. Do not patch rows by hand.
projection handler. Write a test that delivers the same event twice and an older event after a newer one. Assert the row ends at the right status and version."
"List every read model fed from the orders service. For each, show its source, how its checkpoint is stored, and the command to rebuild it from scratch."
"Change the ship-order endpoint to return the new status and stream version. Then change the order page to show that status until a query returns the same version or higher, with a 2-second timeout."
The row update and the checkpoint save are in one transaction.
The handler compares versions. A plain upsert with no version check lets an old event overwrite a new one.
Events for one aggregate cannot be handled by two workers at the same time.
The rebuild path writes to a new table and swaps. It does not truncate the live one.
The rebuild does not send emails or call other services. Those belong to other handlers.
No code in the command path writes to a read store directly.

q.v: A projection handler receives event version 9 for order

options.v: Apply the event again, since the newest event always wins.
Skip it. The event was already applied, so applying it again could double-count.
Throw an error, because a duplicate means the event store is broken.

why.v: Delivery is at least once, so duplicates are normal. A stored version that is equal or higher means the event is already in the row.

q.v: A user clicks "Rename project". The API replies 200, but the list page still shows the old name for a second. Which fix keeps CQRS and removes the confusion?

options.v: Write to the read model directly from the command handler, in a second call.
Return the new state and version from the command, and show it until the read model reaches that version.
Turn off the projection and read from the write model everywhere.

why.v: The command already knows the new state. Showing it, then waiting for the matching version, gives read-your-writes without a dual write.

q.v: You must add a new field to a read model fed by events. What is the safest way to fill it for old data?

options.v: Build a new copy of the read model from the first event, then switch readers to it once it has caught up.
Edit old events in the event store so they include the new field.
Run an UPDATE on the live read-model table and accept a short gap.

why.v: A read model is derived data. Rebuilding it next to the old one, then swapping, keeps readers on a complete view the whole time.

q.v: A team wants CQRS with a separate read database for a settings page with simple create, read, update and delete screens. What should a senior say?

options.v: Yes, CQRS makes every part of a system faster.
No. Simple CRUD fits one model, and CQRS would add lag and moving parts for no gain.
Yes, but only with event sourcing.

why.v: Fowler and Microsoft both say CQRS is a poor fit when the domain is simple and CRUD is enough.
